Chapter 15 · Dividing out the order
Why does ⁿCᵣ divide the ordered count ⁿPᵣ by r!?
Every team of r people can be lined up in r! different orders. Dividing by r! collapses those r! orders into one single team.
The rule: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿPᵣ ÷ r! = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!)
Roll two fair dice and add the spots. Why does a total of 7 show up six times as often as a total of 12?
You roll a red die and a blue die and add them. There are 11 possible totals, from 2 to 12. Does each total have a 1 in 11 chance?
No. A total of 12 happens in only one way, 6 on red and 6 on blue. A total of 7 happens in six ways: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2) and (6,1).
Draw a 6 × 6 grid with red 1 to 6 along the side and blue 1 to 6 along the top. Count the 36 squares, and shade the diagonal of four squares that add to 9: (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3).
Why count the 36 pairs instead of the 11 totals? Each of the 36 pairs is equally likely, 1 in 36. The 11 totals are not equally likely because different numbers of pairs make them.

One possible result of a trial is an outcome, and the complete list or grid of all possible results is the sample space. When outcomes are equally likely, the probability of a result is wanted outcomes ÷ total outcomes, on a scale from 0 to 1. Results that cannot happen at the same time are mutually exclusive; their probabilities add up, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
On the 36-square grid for two fair dice, four squares add to 9. So the probability of a sum of 9 is 4 ÷ 36 = 1/9, and the probability of not getting 9 is 1 − 1/9 = 8/9.
The tempting slip is to treat (3, 6) and (6, 3) as one outcome. Red 3 with blue 6 and red 6 with blue 3 are two separate squares on the 36-square grid.
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that their sum is 11, as a fraction in simplest form?
List the sample space of equally likely outcomes first; probability is wanted outcomes ÷ total outcomes, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue marbles, 8 in all. You pick one marble, keep it out, and pick a second. Why does the fraction for the second marble change?
Because only 7 marbles are left in the bag. If the first marble was red, only 4 of the remaining 7 are red, so the chance of two reds is 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.
Draw two branches from the start labeled Red (5/8) and Blue (3/8). From the Red tip, split into Red (4/7) and Blue (3/7), and multiply along the top path: 5/8 × 4/7.
Why multiply along the branches? Five eighths of the time you take the top branch, and four sevenths of those times you take the next top branch. Four sevenths of five eighths is 5/8 × 4/7.

A probability estimated from real trials, count of successes ÷ number of trials, is an experimental probability. Two stages where the first result does not change the chances of the second are independent events, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). A branching picture that writes each step's fractions on its branches is a tree diagram.
If you put the first marble back before picking the second, the two picks are independent events: P(both red) = 5/8 × 5/8 = 25/64. Without replacement they are not: P(both red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 5/14.
The tempting slip is to add along a path, writing 5/8 + 4/7. Multiply along the branches to follow one path; add at the end only when combining two separate paths.
A bag holds 4 green and 2 yellow counters, 6 in all. Two counters are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are green, in simplest form?
On a tree diagram, multiply along branches for one path and add separate paths. Only independent events keep the same fractions on the second step.
From 8 students, how many ways can you award Gold, Silver and Bronze medals? How does that count change for an equal 3-person team?

For medals, there are 8 choices for Gold, 7 for Silver and 6 for Bronze: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 ways. For a team, the same 3 students can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 medal orders, so divide 336 by 6 to get 56 teams.
Draw three medal boxes [8][7][6]. Underneath, group the 6 rearrangements of Asha, Rohan and Meera into one single team box.
Why divide by 6? In a team there is no Gold, Silver or Bronze. Every group of 3 people was counted 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 times in the ordered list, so dividing by 6 counts each team once.

This section goes beyond the school book. The product of all whole numbers from n down to 1 is n factorial, written n!. An ordered arrangement of r items from n is a permutation, ⁿPᵣ = n! ÷ (n − r)!. An unordered selection of r items from n is a combination, ⁿCᵣ = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!).
4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. To choose 2 captains of equal rank from 6 players, calculate ⁶C₂ = (6 × 5) ÷ (2 × 1) = 15 pairs.
The tempting slip is to use ⁿPᵣ when order does not matter. Ask whether swapping two picked people changes the result: if not, divide by r! to get a combination.
How many different 2-topping pizzas can you choose from 7 toppings, where the order of the two toppings does not matter?
n! multiplies from n down to 1; a permutation counts ordered picks, and a combination divides by r! when order does not matter.
A ball drops through 6 rows of pegs, bouncing left or right with a 50% chance at each peg. Why do most balls pile up in the middle slots instead of spreading evenly across the bottom?
Because there is only 1 path that goes right all 6 times, but there are ⁶C₃ = 20 different paths that go right 3 times and left 3 times.
In the figure, set the pegboard rows to 6, the slot to 3, and the bounce chance to 50%. Read the path counts above the bars: 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1, adding up to 64 paths in all.
Why is the count in slot k equal to ⁿCₖ? Choosing a path to slot k means choosing which k of the n rows bounce right. That is a combination of k rows out of n.
As the number of rows grows, the tall middle bars and low outer tails smooth into the symmetric shape called a bell curve.
With 6 rows at 50%, there are 2⁶ = 64 equally likely paths. Slot 3 has ⁶C₃ = 20 paths, so the probability of landing in slot 3 is 20 ÷ 64 = 5/16 = 31.25%.
The tempting slip is to think a ball 'aims' for the middle. Every single path has the same 1 in 64 chance; the middle wins only because 20 paths lead there.
A ball drops through 4 rows of pegs (n = 4). How many paths ⁴C₂ land in the middle slot (k = 2)?
Slot k after n rows of pegs collects ⁿCₖ paths, piling most balls in the middle to form a bell curve.

With no calculator: out of 1,000 people, 2% (20 people) have a trait and 980 do not. A test flags 95% of the 20 who have it, and also falsely flags 5% of the 980 who do not. How many people test positive in all, and what fraction of them actually have the trait?
95% of 20 is 19 true positives, and 5% of 980 is 49 false positives. In all, 19 + 49 = 68 people test positive, and 19/68 (about 27.9%) actually have the trait.

In a school of 1,000 students, 20 cycle to school and 980 walk or take the bus. What is the chance a student cycles before you look, and how does it change if they hold a cycle helmet?
Before you see the helmet, the chance is 20 out of 1,000, or 2%. Once you see the helmet, you stop dividing by all 1,000 students and divide only by the students carrying a helmet.

The starting share of a group in the whole population, such as 20 in 1,000 (2%), is the base rate. Your starting probability before seeing the clue is the prior. The probability of A given that B has happened is the conditional probability, written P(A | B), read 'the probability of A given B'.
In a two-way table, 30 students play chess, and 12 of those 30 also play tabla. Given that a student plays chess, the conditional probability they play tabla is 12 ÷ 30 = 2/5.
The tempting slip is to keep dividing by the whole 1,000 after you know the clue happened. The vertical bar in P(A | B) means 'restrict the denominator to B'.
In a club of 100 members, 25 wear glasses, and 10 of those 25 are left-handed. Given that a member wears glasses, what is the conditional probability they are left-handed, in simplest form?

Out of 1,000 people, 20 are sick and 980 are healthy. A test catches 95% of the 20 sick people, and it is 95% accurate on the 980 healthy people too. How many healthy people still get a wrong positive result?
5% of 980, which is 49 healthy people. Even a small 5% slip rate makes a big pile of 49 wrong alarms when it acts on a crowd of 980 healthy people.
Split a bar of 1,000 people into 20 sick on the left and 980 healthy on the right. Colour 19 of the 20 red (0.95 × 20 = 19), and colour 49 of the 980 amber (0.05 × 980 = 49).
Why are there more amber boxes (49) than red boxes (19)? Because healthy people outnumber sick people 980 to 20. Five per cent of a huge crowd beats ninety-five per cent of a tiny group.

The share of sick people the test rightly flags positive is its sensitivity (here 19 out of 20, or 95%). The share of healthy people the test rightly clears negative is its specificity (here 931 out of 980, or 95%). A healthy person wrongly flagged positive is a false positive (here the remaining 5% of 980, which is 49 people).
If 500 people are healthy and a test has 98% specificity, then 98% of 500 = 490 test negative, and the remaining 2% of 500 = 10 are false positives.
The tempting slip is to take 5% of all 1,000 people instead of 5% of the 980 healthy people. Sensitivity acts on the sick group; the false-positive rate acts on the healthy group.
Out of 400 healthy people, a test has a 5% false-positive rate (95% specificity). How many false positives does it produce?
Sensitivity measures true hits among the sick; specificity measures true clears among the healthy, and the rest of the healthy group are false positives.
Put all 19 truly sick positive testers and all 49 false-positive testers into one room. If you are in that room of 68 people, what is the chance you are actually sick?
19 out of 68, which is about 27.9%. The 932 people who tested negative are not in the room, so the chance is red divided by red plus amber.
In the figure, look at the stacked bar on the far right for 2%, 95% and 5%. The red top piece is 19 and the amber bottom piece is 49, making 68 positive tests in all.

Why did the chance jump from 2% to 27.9%, yet stop far short of 95%? A positive test is 95% ÷ 5% = 19 times as likely when you are sick as when you are healthy, which boosts the odds from 20 : 980 to (20 × 19) : 980 = 380 : 980 = 19 : 49.

The updated probability after seeing the evidence is the posterior. The multiplier sensitivity ÷ false-positive rate (here 95% ÷ 5% = 19) is the likelihood ratio. The rule posterior = true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives) is Bayes' theorem.
In a group of 1,000 people, 10 are sick and 990 are healthy. A test flags 9 of the 10 sick people and 9 of the 990 healthy people. By Bayes' theorem, the posterior is 9 ÷ (9 + 9) = 9/18 = 1/2 = 50%.
The tempting slip is to confuse the test's 95% sensitivity with the posterior. Forgetting the base rate and assuming P(sick | +) equals P(+ | sick) is the base-rate trap.
In a screening of 1,000 people, there are 20 true positives and 60 false positives. What is the posterior probability of being sick given a positive test, as a decimal?
Bayes' theorem finds the posterior by dividing true positives by all positives (true positives + false positives), multiplying the prior odds by the likelihood ratio.

A straight line cutting through two points on a curve is a secant line. The value that an expression approaches as the step shrinks toward zero is the limit. The line that touches the curve at one point with that exact limiting slope is the tangent line.
On y = x² between x = 3 and x = 3.1 (so h = 0.1), the secant line has slope (9.61 − 9) ÷ 0.1 = 6.1. At h = 0.01 it is 6.01, and the limit as h approaches 0 gives a tangent line of slope 6.

A secant line joins two points step h apart; taking the limit as h shrinks to 0 turns it into the tangent line at one point.

A stone dropped from a cliff falls y = 5t² metres in t seconds. Between t = 1 and t = 3 it falls 40 metres in 2 seconds, an average of 20 m/s. How fast is it falling at the exact instant t = 2 seconds?

Why does a car's speedometer match the slope of the tangent line? A speedometer measures distance ÷ time over a tiny fraction of a second, which is the tangent slope at that moment.

How fast one quantity changes per unit of another at a single instant is the rate of change. The rule or function that gives the tangent slope at any point x is the derivative, written f′(x) or dy/dx.
For y = 5t², the derivative is dy/dt = 10t. At t = 1 s the stone falls at 10 m/s; at t = 2 s it falls at 20 m/s; at t = 3 s it falls at 30 m/s.

The tempting slip is to divide total height by total time, y ÷ t, as if the graph were a straight line from (0, 0). At t = 2 on y = 5t², y ÷ t gives 20 ÷ 2 = 10 m/s, which is only the average from t = 0 to t = 2, half the instantaneous speed of 20 m/s.

The derivative dy/dx or f′(x) gives the instantaneous rate of change, the slope of the tangent line at x.

Bringing the exponent n down in front and reducing the exponent by 1 is the power rule. The derivative of xⁿ is n xⁿ⁻¹.
By the power rule, the derivative of x⁴ is 4x³. For y = 3x² + 5x − 7, the derivative is dy/dx = 3(2x) + 5(1) − 0 = 6x + 5, because a constant −7 does not change.
The tempting slip is to bring the power down and forget to subtract 1 from the exponent, writing 3x³ for the derivative of x³. Always drop the exponent by 1: x³ becomes 3x².

A point on a curve where the derivative dy/dx equals 0 is a stationary point. A peak is a local maximum and a valley is a local minimum; together they are maximum and minimum points.
A ball's height is h(t) = 20t − 5t². Its derivative is dh/dt = 20 − 10t. Setting 20 − 10t = 0 gives t = 2 seconds, and the peak height is h(2) = 20(2) − 5(4) = 20 metres.

At a stationary point the tangent line is horizontal (dy/dx = 0), marking a smooth maximum and minimum.

The limit of the Riemann sum from x = a to x = b as strip width shrinks to 0 is the definite integral, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. The elongated S sign ∫ stands for 'sum'. Because regions above the x-axis count as positive and regions below count as negative, the definite integral measures signed area.
Under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = 3, the region is a triangle of base 3 and height 6. So the definite integral ∫₀³ 2x dx = ½ × 3 × 6 = 9.

Suppose you know a train's speed at every instant is v(t) = 2t, and you notice that the position rule F(t) = t² has derivative F′(t) = 2t. How can F(t) = t² give you the area under v(t) = 2t from t = 1 to t = 4 in one subtraction?
Each thin strip of area under the speed curve, v(t) × dt, is a tiny step of distance dF. Adding all the tiny steps from t = 1 to t = 4 gives the total change in position: F(4) − F(1) = 4² − 1² = 15.
Stack thin vertical steps dF one on top of another from F(a) up to F(b). The middle steps cancel in pairs, leaving only F(b) − F(a).
How do you reverse the power rule to find F(x) from xⁿ? Differentiating multiplied by the power and subtracted 1; reversing it adds 1 to the power and divides by the new power: xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1).
A function F(x) whose derivative F′(x) equals f(x) is an antiderivative of f(x). The rule that the definite integral of f(x) from a to b equals F(b) − F(a) is the fundamental theorem of calculus.
To find ∫₀² 3x² dx, notice that x³ has derivative 3x², so F(x) = x³ is an antiderivative. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the exact area is F(2) − F(0) = 2³ − 0³ = 8.

The tempting slip when finding an antiderivative of xⁿ is to subtract 1 from the power as if differentiating. Always add 1 to the exponent and divide by the new exponent, then check by differentiating your answer.
Since F(x) = x³ is an antiderivative of 3x², use F(3) − F(1) to find the exact area ∫₁³ 3x² dx.
An antiderivative F(x) reverses the derivative, and the fundamental theorem of calculus says ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

A non-zero vector v that a matrix A stretches without turning, so that Av = λv, is an eigenvector of A. The scale factor λ (the Greek letter lambda) is its eigenvalue.

Step 4: So ∠ACD = 4 × 40 − 5 = 155°. Check: ∠BAC = 95° and ∠ABC = 60°, and 95 + 60 = 155.
Find the midpoint M of the line segment joining A(−4, 7) and B(10, −3).

Step 1: Add the x-coordinates and halve: (−4 + 10) ÷ 2 = 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
Step 2: Add the y-coordinates and halve: (7 + (−3)) ÷ 2 = 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
Step 3: So M = (3, 2).
Step 4: Check: from A to M is 7 across and 5 down, and from M to B is 7 across and 5 down too.
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. The co-interior angles are (3y + 10)° and (2y − 5)°. Find y.

Step 1: Co-interior angles add to 180°, so (3y + 10) + (2y − 5) = 180.
Step 2: Collect like terms: 5y + 5 = 180.
Step 3: Take 5 from both sides: 5y = 175, so y = 35.
Step 4: Check: the angles are 115° and 65°, and 115 + 65 = 180.
Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 156°. How many sides n does the polygon have?

Step 1: Each exterior angle is 180° − 156° = 24°.
Step 2: The exterior angles of a polygon add to 360°, one at each corner.
Step 3: So there are 360 ÷ 24 = 15 corners, and 15 sides.
Step 4: Check: (15 − 2) × 180° = 2340°, and 2340 ÷ 15 = 156.
Each exterior angle is 180° − 156° = 24°, so the number of sides is 360 ÷ 24 = ___.
After a 15% monsoon discount, a jacket costs ₹2,040. Using a reverse-percentage multiplier, find its original price before the discount.

Step 1: A 15% discount leaves 100% − 15% = 85% of the old price. The multiplier is 0.85.
Step 2: So the old price × 0.85 = ₹2,040.
Step 3: To undo × 0.85, divide by 0.85. Multiply both numbers by 100 first: 204,000 ÷ 85 = 2,400.
Step 4: The old price was ₹2,400. Check forwards: ₹2,400 × 0.85 = ₹2,040.
The old price × 0.85 = ₹2,040, so the old price is ₹2,040 ÷ 0.85 = ___.
Evaluate 36 ÷ 0.15 without a calculator.

Step 1: You are dividing by a number less than 1, so expect an answer bigger than 36.
Step 2: Multiply both numbers by 100 to clear the decimal. 36 ÷ 0.15 becomes 3,600 ÷ 15.
Step 3: 15 × 24 = 360, so 360 ÷ 15 = 24 and 3,600 ÷ 15 = 240.
Step 4: Check: 240 × 0.15 = 36.
36 ÷ 0.15 is the same as 3,600 ÷ 15, which is ___.
A price increases by 20% and then decreases by 20%. What is the net percentage change?

Step 1: A 20% rise has the multiplier 1.2.
Step 2: A 20% fall has the multiplier 0.8.
Step 3: Changes in a row multiply. 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96.
Step 4: 0.96 is 96% of the starting price, so the price has fallen by 4%. The overall change is −4%.
The two multipliers are 1.2 and 0.8. Multiply them and compare with 1. The overall change is ___.
₹50,000 is invested at 10% per annum compound interest for 3 years. Find the total interest earned.

Step 1: The multiplier for 10% growth is 1.1.
Step 2: Year 1: ₹50,000 × 1.1 = ₹55,000.
Step 3: Year 2: ₹55,000 × 1.1 = ₹60,500. Year 3: ₹60,500 × 1.1 = ₹66,550.
Step 4: The interest is the final amount take away the start. ₹66,550 − ₹50,000 = ₹16,550.
After 3 years the ₹50,000 has grown to ₹66,550. The interest earned is ___.
In a continuous mass survey, the class interval 40 ≤ m < 60 kg has frequency 30, and 60 ≤ m < 70 kg has frequency 25. Calculate the Frequency Density of each class.

Step 1: The first class 40 ≤ m < 60 kg has class width 60 − 40 = 20 kg, so its frequency density is 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.
Step 2: The second class 60 ≤ m < 70 kg has class width 70 − 60 = 10 kg, so its frequency density is 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5.
Step 3: The second class has fewer items in total, but they are packed more tightly per kilogram.
First class: 30 ÷ 20 = ___. Second class: 25 ÷ 10 = ___.
Find the median and interquartile range (IQR) of the ordered dataset: 12, 15, 17, 20, 24, 29, 31.

Step 1: There are 7 ordered values: 12, 15, 17, 20, 24, 29, 31. The middle (4th) value is the median, 20.
Step 2: The lower half 12, 15, 17 has middle Q₁ = 15, and the upper half 24, 29, 31 has middle Q₃ = 29.
Step 3: The interquartile range is Q₃ − Q₁ = 29 − 15 = 14.
The middle value is the median = ___, and Q₃ − Q₁ = 29 − 15 = ___.
Compute the population standard deviation σ of the five numbers: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.

Step 1: Find the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12: (4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12) ÷ 5 = 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
Step 2: Square the gaps from 8: (−4)² + (−2)² + 0² + 2² + 4² = 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40.
Step 3: Divide by 5 to get variance 8, then take the square root: σ = √8 ≈ 2.83.
Mean = 8, variance = 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so standard deviation σ = √8 ≈ ___.
A histogram bar for 10 ≤ t < 25 s has Frequency Density 3.2. How many observations lie in this class?

Step 1: The class 10 ≤ t < 25 s has class width 25 − 10 = 15 seconds.
Step 2: Count = frequency density × class width = 3.2 × 15 = 48 observations.
Class width = 25 − 10 = 15 s, so the count is 15 × 3.2 = ___.
Find the nth term formula Tₙ of the linear sequence 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, … and calculate the sum S₂₀ of its first 20 terms using Gauss's pairing method.

Step 1: The gaps are all 4, so start from 4n: 4, 8, 12. Each term is 3 more, so Tₙ = 4n + 3.
Step 2: The 20th term is 4 × 20 + 3 = 83.
Step 3: Pair the first and last terms. There are 20 terms, so 10 pairs of 7 + 83 = 90.
Step 4: The sum of the first 20 terms is 10 × 90 = 900.
Tₙ = 4n + 3 and the 20th term is 83. The sum is 10 × (7 + 83) = ___.
Does the number 150 belong to the sequence Tₙ = 4n + 3? Justify your answer algebraically.

Step 1: Set the nth term equal to 150. 4n + 3 = 150.
Step 2: Take 3 from both sides. 4n = 147.
Step 3: Divide by 4. n = 36.75, which is not a whole number.
Step 4: So 150 is not a term. The 36th term is 147 and the 37th is 151.
4n + 3 = 150 gives 4n = 147 and n = ___, so 150 ___ a term.
Find the nth term of the quadratic sequence 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, …

Step 1: The first differences are 5, 7, 9, 11, and the second differences are all 2.
Step 2: Half of 2 is 1, so start from n²: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
Step 3: Take n² away from each term: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That is 2n.
Step 4: So Tₙ = n² + 2n. Check the 5th term: 25 + 10 = 35.
The terms minus n² are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, so Tₙ = n² + ___.
Using Gauss's staircase formula, evaluate 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 200.

Step 1: Pair the first number with the last. 1 + 200 = 201, and 2 + 199 = 201.
Step 2: There are 200 numbers, so there are 100 pairs.
Step 3: The sum is 100 × 201 = 20,100.
Step 4: Check with the rule n(n + 1) ÷ 2: 200 × 201 ÷ 2 = 20,100.
100 pairs, each adding to 201, make ___.
Kym, Aarav, and Meera share a prize in the ratio 3 : 5 : 8. Given that Meera receives ₹1,350 more than Kym, find the total prize using a Singapore Bar Model.

Step 1: Meera has 8 parts and Kym has 3 parts, so Meera has 8 − 3 = 5 parts more.
Step 2: Those 5 parts are the ₹1,350. So 1 part = ₹1,350 ÷ 5 = ₹270.
Step 3: There are 3 + 5 + 8 = 16 parts in all.
Step 4: The total prize is 16 × ₹270 = ₹4,320.
5 parts = ₹1,350, so 1 part = ₹270. All 16 parts together make ___.
Convert 3.5 m² into cm².

Step 1: 1 m = 100 cm.
Step 2: A square 1 m by 1 m is 100 cm by 100 cm. So 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm².
Step 3: Multiply the area by 10,000. 3.5 × 10,000 = 35,000.
Step 4: 3.5 m² = 35,000 cm².
6 pumps working together empty a flooded basement in 10 hours. How long will 15 identical pumps take?

Step 1: More pumps share the same job, so the time goes down. This is inverse proportion.
Step 2: Find the whole job. 6 pumps × 10 hours = 60 hours of work for one pump.
Step 3: Share the job among 15 pumps. 60 ÷ 15 = 4.
Step 4: 15 pumps take 4 hours. Check: 15 × 4 = 60, the same job.
The job is 6 × 10 = 60 hours of work for one pump. With 15 pumps it takes ___.
The ratio A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 6 : 7. Find the combined three-way ratio A : B : C in simplest integer form.

Step 1: B is 4 in one ratio and 6 in the other. The lowest common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12.
Step 2: Multiply both parts of 3 : 4 by 3, so that B becomes 12. A : B = 9 : 12.
Step 3: Multiply both parts of 6 : 7 by 2, so that B becomes 12. B : C = 12 : 14.
Step 4: B now matches, so join them. A : B : C = 9 : 12 : 14. No factor divides all three, so stop.
Triangle T has area 6 cm² and vertex A(2, 3). It is enlarged by scale factor k = 3 about centre C(1, 1). Find the coordinates of image A′ and the area of image T′.

Step 1: The step from C(1, 1) to A(2, 3) is 1 across and 2 up.
Step 2: Multiply the step by the scale factor 3: 3 across and 6 up.
Step 3: Add it to C. The image of A is at (1 + 3, 1 + 6) = (4, 7).
Step 4: The area is multiplied by 3² = 9, so the image has area 9 × 6 = 54 cm².
The step from C to A is 1 across and 2 up, so the step to its image is 3 across and 6 up. The image of A is at (4, 7), and the area is 3² × 6 = ___ cm².
Reflect the point P(−3, 5) in the line y = x.

Step 1: The line y = x runs through (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 2), at 45° to the axes.
Step 2: Reflecting in it swaps the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate.
Step 3: So P(−3, 5) goes to (5, −3).
Step 4: Check: halfway between P and P′ is (1, 1), which is on the mirror line.
Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates, so P(−3, 5) goes to P′ = ___.
Rotate the point Q(4, 1) by 90° anticlockwise about the origin (0, 0).

Step 1: Q is 4 across and 1 up from the centre (0, 0).
Step 2: A quarter turn anticlockwise turns a step across into a step up, and a step up into a step left.
Step 3: So 4 across becomes 4 up, and 1 up becomes 1 to the left.
Step 4: Q′ = (−1, 4). Check: Q and Q′ are the same distance from (0, 0).
Q is 4 across and 1 up. After a quarter turn anticlockwise it is 1 to the left and 4 up, so Q′ = ___.
Enlarge the point R(5, 3) by negative scale factor k = −2 about centre C(3, 2).

Step 1: The step from C(3, 2) to R(5, 3) is 2 across and 1 up.
Step 2: Multiply the step by −2: 4 to the left and 2 down.
Step 3: Add it to C: R′ = (3 − 4, 2 − 2) = (−1, 0).
Step 4: A negative scale factor puts the image on the other side of the centre, upside down.
The step from C to R is 2 across and 1 up. Times −2 it is 4 left and 2 down, so R′ = ___.
Find the equation of the straight line passing through A(−2, 1) and B(4, 13) in the form y = mx + c, and state where it crosses the x-axis.

Step 1: The gradient is (13 − 1) ÷ (4 − (−2)) = 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
Step 2: So the line is y = 2x + c. Put in (4, 13): 13 = 8 + c, so c = 5 and y = 2x + 5.
Step 3: Check with (−2, 1): 2 × (−2) + 5 = 1.
Step 4: For the x-intercept, set y = 0. 2x + 5 = 0, so x = −2.5.
The line is y = 2x + 5. Setting y = 0 gives 2x = −5, so x = ___.
For the function f(x) = 3x − 7, find the inverse function f⁻¹(x).

Step 1: The machine for f(x) = 3x − 7 multiplies by 3, then takes 7.
Step 2: Undo the steps in reverse order: first add 7, then divide by 3.
Step 3: So f⁻¹(x) = (x + 7) ÷ 3.
Step 4: Check: f(4) = 5, and f⁻¹(5) = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
f(x) = 3x − 7 multiplies by 3, then takes 7. So f⁻¹(x) = (x + ___) ÷ 3.
Find the equation of the line perpendicular to y = 2x + 5 that passes through (0, 3).

Step 1: y = 2x + 5 has gradient 2.
Step 2: A perpendicular gradient multiplies with 2 to give −1, so it is −½.
Step 3: The line passes through (0, 3), so it crosses the y-axis at 3.
Step 4: The line is y = −½x + 3. Check: 2 × (−½) = −1.
2 × m = −1 gives m = −½, and the line crosses the y-axis at 3, so y = ___x + 3.
Find the point of intersection of the lines y = 3x − 2 and x + 2y = 10.

Step 1: Put y = 3x − 2 into x + 2y = 10. x + 2(3x − 2) = 10.
Step 2: Expand the brackets. x + 6x − 4 = 10, so 7x = 14 and x = 2.
Step 3: Then y = 3 × 2 − 2 = 4.
Step 4: The lines meet at (2, 4). Check: 2 + 2 × 4 = 10.
7x = 14 gives x = 2, and y = 3 × 2 − 2 = ___, so the lines meet at (2, ___).

A rare genetic trait occurs in 2% of a population (P(D) = 0.02). A screening test has 95% sensitivity (P(+|D) = 0.95) and a 5% false-positive rate (P(+|¬D) = 0.05). Out of 1,000 people, find the number of True Positives, False Positives, and P(D | +).

Step 1: Out of 1,000 people, 2% have the trait: 0.02 × 1,000 = 20 people, and 980 do not.
Step 2: True positives = 95% of 20 = 0.95 × 20 = 19 people.
Step 3: False positives = 5% of 980 = 0.05 × 980 = 49 people.
Step 4: Out of 19 + 49 = 68 positive tests, P(D | +) = 19/68 ≈ 27.9%.
True positives = 19 and false positives = 49, so P(D | +) = 19 ÷ (19 + 49) = ___.
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that their sum is 9?

Step 1: Two six-sided dice have 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely pairs in the sample space.
Step 2: List the pairs that add to 9: (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4) and (6, 3), which is 4 pairs.
Step 3: Divide 4 by 36 and simplify: 4/36 = 1/9.
4 pairs out of 36 add to 9, so the probability is 4/36 = ___.
A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.

Step 1: On the first draw there are 5 red marbles out of 8, so P(1st red) = 5/8.
Step 2: Without replacement, 4 red marbles remain out of 7, so P(2nd red) = 4/7.
Step 3: Multiply along the branch: 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.
5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = ___ in simplest form.
How many 3-person committees can be chosen from 8 students (⁸C₃)?

Step 1: There are 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 ordered ways to pick 3 students from 8.
Step 2: A committee has no order, and 3 students can be ordered in 3! = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways.
Step 3: Divide 336 by 6: ⁸C₃ = 336 ÷ 6 = 56 committees.
Given column vectors a = (3, 4)ᵀ and b = (2, −1)ᵀ, calculate 2a − 3b and find the exact magnitude |a|.

Step 1: Scale each vector: 2a = 2(3, 4) = (6, 8) and 3b = 3(2, −1) = (6, −3).
Step 2: Subtract component by component: 2a − 3b = (6 − 6, 8 − (−3)) = (0, 11).
Step 3: By Pythagoras' theorem, |a| = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.
If AB = (4, −2)ᵀ and BC = (−1, 7)ᵀ, find the resultant vector AC.

Step 1: Chain the journeys nose to tail using the triangle law: AC = AB + BC.
Step 2: Add the horizontal and vertical components: (4 + (−1), −2 + 7) = (3, 5).
In triangle OAB, OA = a, OB = b, M is the midpoint of OA, and N is the midpoint of OB. Express MN in terms of a and b.

Step 1: Since M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB, OM = ½a and ON = ½b.
Step 2: Go from M to O and then from O to N: MN = −OM + ON = −½a + ½b = ½(b − a).
MN = ON − OM = ½b − ½a = ___.
Calculate the determinant det(A) = ad − bc of the 2×2 transformation matrix A = [[3, 1], [2, 4]], and state how much it scales the area of a triangle of area 5 cm².

Step 1: For A = [[3, 1], [2, 4]], the determinant is det(A) = (3 × 4) − (1 × 2) = 12 − 2 = 10.
Step 2: The determinant is the area scale factor of the transformation.
Step 3: Multiply the original triangle's area by 10: 10 × 5 cm² = 50 cm².
det(A) = (3 × 4) − (1 × 2) = ___, so the new area is 10 × 5 = ___ cm².
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number turns the sign round on the number line. Two negative signs make a positive; one negative and one positive make a negative.

A square number is a whole number multiplied by itself, and a cube number is multiplied by itself three times. In prime factors, a square has even powers and a cube has powers that are multiples of 3.
When multiplying powers of the same base, add the indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. When dividing, subtract the indices: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, and a⁰ = 1.
Break each number into prime factors with a factor tree. The highest common factor (HCF) multiplies the shared primes; the lowest common multiple (LCM) takes each prime the most times it appears.
Work out brackets and powers before multiplying and dividing, and add or subtract last. Notice that (−3)² = +9, whereas −3² means −(3 × 3) = −9.
Whole numbers, negative numbers and fractions are rational numbers, which stop or repeat as decimals. A square root of a non-square whole number, such as √2, is an irrational number.
An expression has no = sign, such as 3x + 2. An equation is true for only some values of x, such as 3x + 2 = 11. An identity is true for every value, such as 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2.
A number outside a bracket multiplies each term inside, signs included: −3(x − 5) = −3x + 15. For two brackets, multiply each term of one by each term of the other, then collect like terms.
Take the HCF of every term outside a bracket, numbers and letters both: 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Then check that nothing common is left inside. A difference of two squares factorises as (a − b)(a + b).
Put each number in a bracket as you substitute it. When x = −4, x² is (−4)² = 16, but −x² is −16. Work out powers before you multiply.
A quadrilateral has four sides, and its angles add to 360°. A rhombus and a kite have diagonals that cross at right angles, and a rectangle has diagonals of equal length.
A net of a solid folds up into it, and the plan view and elevations show it from above, the front and the side. For a solid with no holes, Euler's formula says V − E + F = 2.
A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures, from 000° to 359°. The back bearing differs by 180°, so 065° gives 245°.
Three sides (SSS), two sides and the angle between them (SAS), or two angles and the side between them (ASA) fix a triangle. Triangles that match in one of these ways are congruent.
The perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equally far from A and B. An angle bisector is the locus of points equally far from the two arms of the angle.

Primary data is data you collect yourself by counting, measuring or asking questions. Secondary data comes from a table or record someone else already gathered. A fair questionnaire uses short, neutral questions and non-overlapping answer boxes that cover every possible reply.

A random sample gives every member of the population the same chance. A systematic sample picks every kth member from a numbered list, and a stratified sample takes from each group in proportion to its size.
The circumference of a circle is π times its diameter, C = πd = 2πr, with π about 3.14. A sector with angle θ has θ/360 of the circle's area and of its circumference.
A parallelogram's area is base × height. A trapezium's area is ½(a + b) × h. In both, the height is measured at a right angle to the base.
The volume of a prism is the area of its cross-section × its length. A triangular prism with a 12 cm² triangle at each end and a length of 20 cm holds 240 cm³.
The surface area of a solid adds up the areas of all its faces. Draw its net, find the area of each face, and add them.
Some lengths, weights and amounts are still given in older units. 5 miles is about 8 km, 1 inch is about 2.5 cm, 1 kg is about 2.2 pounds, and 1 litre is about 1.76 pints.
Multiply decimals as whole numbers, then count the decimal places back in. To divide by a decimal, first multiply both numbers by 10 or 100 so you divide by a whole number.
Significant figures are counted from the first digit that is not zero. Round once, at the end of a calculation.

A fraction in simplest form gives a decimal that stops only when its denominator is built from 2s and 5s. Otherwise the digits repeat. To turn a recurring decimal into a fraction, multiply so the repeating tails line up, then subtract.
Write both mixed numbers as improper fractions. Give them a common denominator, then subtract the numerators.
To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
Turn words or a diagram into a formula. Give each quantity a letter and a unit. A rectangle L cm long and w cm wide has perimeter P = 2(L + w).
Do the same to both sides. Expand any brackets, and clear a fraction by multiplying both sides by its bottom number. Gather the letter terms on one side, then check the answer in the first equation.
To change the subject, undo the steps in reverse order on both sides. If the new subject appears twice, gather both terms on one side and factorise to take it out.
Solve an inequality like an equation. On a number line, < and > get an open circle, and ≤ and ≥ a filled dot. Multiplying or dividing by a negative number turns the sign round.
An exterior angle of a triangle lies between one side carried on and the next side. It equals the sum of the angles at the other two corners, so angles of 50° and 70° give an exterior angle of 120°.

Where two lines cross, vertically opposite angles are equal. When a transversal cuts parallel lines, corresponding angles (F) and alternate angles (Z) are equal, and co-interior angles (C) add to 180°.
The midpoint of a line segment averages the coordinates of its ends. The midpoint of (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is ((x₁ + x₂) ÷ 2, (y₁ + y₂) ÷ 2).
Multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive amount smaller. 0.4 of something is less than all of it.
Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive amount bigger. Scale both numbers up until you divide by a whole number: 7 ÷ 0.25 is 700 ÷ 25.
A percentage change is one multiplication. A 15% rise is × 1.15 and a 15% fall is × 0.85. To go back to the old amount, divide by the multiplier. Changes in a row multiply.
Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways to write one number: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. Pick the form that makes the sum shortest.
A time series graph plots measurements in time order with time on the horizontal axis. A moving average averages fixed-length windows to smooth regular seasonal swings and show the trend.
A stem-and-leaf diagram splits each number into a leading stem and a trailing leaf written in order, with a key. Back-to-back diagrams compare two groups on the same stems.
A histogram shows continuous grouped data with no gaps between bars. When class widths differ, bar height is frequency density = count ÷ class width, so bar area equals the count.
To compare two distributions fairly, compare one measure of middle (mean or median) and one measure of spread (interquartile range or standard deviation).
A term-to-term rule makes each term from the one before, like add 4 or multiply by 2. Equal gaps make an arithmetic sequence. Multiplying by the same number each time makes a geometric sequence.

The nth term gives any term from its position n. For equal gaps d it is dn + c. Equal second differences give a quadratic sequence with an n². To add an arithmetic sequence, multiply the number of terms by the first plus the last, then halve.
A length in metres is 100 times as many centimetres. An area has two lengths, so multiply by 100 twice: 1 m² = 10,000 cm². A volume has three, so 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³.
Put both amounts in the same unit first. Then divide every part of the ratio by a common factor until no more will go.
Add the parts, find what one part is worth, then multiply for each share. If you are told a difference and not the total, match it to the difference in parts.
In direct proportion, both amounts are multiplied by the same number. In inverse proportion, one is multiplied and the other is divided, so multiplying them together always gives the same answer.
A translation slides a shape without turning it. It is written as a column vector, the step across on top and the step up below. The shape's size and the way it faces stay the same.
A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line. Each point and its image are the same distance from the mirror, measured at a right angle. Reflecting in the line y = x swaps the two coordinates.
A rotation turns a shape about a centre of rotation. To describe one, give the centre, the angle, and clockwise or anticlockwise.
A line of symmetry flips a shape onto itself. The order of rotational symmetry counts how many times a shape fits onto itself in one full turn. A cube can be cut into two mirror halves in 9 ways.
An enlargement multiplies every distance from the centre of enlargement by the scale factor k. Lengths are multiplied by k, areas by k² and volumes by k³.
A function machine follows a rule step by step, like f(x) = 2x + 3. Its inverse undoes the steps in reverse order, so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3) ÷ 2.

The line y = mx + c has gradient m, the change in y divided by the change in x, and crosses the y-axis at (0, c). Parallel lines have the same gradient. Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1. Two lines meet at the point that fits both equations.
A real-life graph shows a steady rate as a straight line. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed, and a flat part means standing still.

Probability measures how likely an outcome is on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). When outcomes cannot happen together they are mutually exclusive, their probabilities add up, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
Experimental probability is successes ÷ trials. As you run more trials, the experimental probability settles closer to the theoretical probability.
When all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely, P(A) = wanted outcomes ÷ total outcomes. Factorials, permutations and combinations count large sample spaces without listing every item.
Two-way sample-space grids and tree diagrams organise combined events. Multiply along branches to find the probability of a path, and add separate paths at the end.
A vector has both magnitude (length) and direction, written as a column vector (x, y). Multiplying by a scalar scales both components, and the magnitude is |v| = √(x² + y²) by Pythagoras' theorem.
Vectors add nose to tail by the triangle law AB + BC = AC, and AB = OB − OA. Showing one vector is a scalar multiple of another proves they are parallel, or collinear if they share a point.

Same signs make a positive and different signs make a negative, so (−3) × (−2) = 6 and 6 ÷ (−3) = −2, and a minus sign stays with its number through every step. Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number turns the sign round: −x < 2 becomes x > −2.

Undo the last step first and do the same to both sides. For x/2 + 3 = 8, take 3 from both sides to get x/2 = 5, then multiply by 2 to get x = 10. An inverse function f⁻¹ makes those undo steps; it is not 1 ÷ f.
The number outside a bracket multiplies each term inside it: −3(x − 4) = −3x + 12. A squared bracket is two brackets, so (x + 2)² = (x + 2)(x + 2) = x² + 4x + 4, not x² + 4.

The HCF is the biggest number that divides both, and the LCM is the smallest number both divide into. For 4 and 10, the HCF is 2 and the LCM is 20, not 4 × 10 = 40. Cancel a fraction by the HCF so nothing common is left, as in 10/15 = 2/3.

Squaring multiplies a number by itself, so 5² = 5 × 5 = 25, not 10, and a square root undoes it: √25 = 5. In a right-angled triangle, square the two shorter sides, add, then take the square root: 3² + 4² = 25, so the longest side is 5.
Add or subtract fractions only once they share a denominator: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6, never 2/5. Turn a mixed number into an improper fraction first, so 1 1/2 is 3/2.

Look at the digit after the last one you keep and round up if it is 5 or more, so 2.367 to 2 decimal places is 2.37, not 2.36. Significant figures start at the first digit that is not zero: 0.005281 to 2 significant figures is 0.0053.

Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left, so 0.47 × 100 = 47, and a recurring decimal never stops, so 10 × 0.333… take away 0.333… is exactly 3. To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by 10 until it is whole: 12 ÷ 0.3 = 120 ÷ 3 = 40.
Ask what one of something is worth: if 4 pens cost £6, one pen costs 6 ÷ 4 = £1.50, and the amount you share out goes first. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a bigger answer, so 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4.

Find one part first: to share 45 in the ratio 4 : 5, there are 9 parts, so one part is 5 and the shares are 20 and 25. If more workers do the same job, it takes less time: 2 workers taking 6 hours means 1 worker takes 12 hours.

A percentage change is one multiplication: a 30% decrease is × 0.7 and a 5% increase is × 1.05. Two changes multiply, so up 40% then down 40% is × 1.4 × 0.6 = × 0.84, and to undo a change you divide by its multiplier.

Change every length to the same unit before you calculate: 1 m = 100 cm, so 3.2 m = 320 cm. An area scales by the square of the length factor, so 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm², and doubling every length makes an area 4 times as big.

A triangle's area is half of base × perpendicular height, so base 6 cm and height 4 cm give 12 cm², and a slanted side is never the height. Use the radius in πr², and add every edge for a perimeter: a quarter circle of radius 2 cm has perimeter π + 4.

Co-interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°. An exterior angle of a polygon is 180° take away the interior angle, so an interior angle of 108° has exterior angle 72°. A back-bearing is the bearing plus 180°, or minus 180° if that passes 360°: the back-bearing of 050° is 230°.

The midpoint averages the x-coordinates and then the y-coordinates, keeping x first: the midpoint of (1, 2) and (5, 10) is (3, 6). Gradient is change in y ÷ change in x, and a perpendicular gradient flips it and changes its sign, so 2/3 becomes −3/2.

Check the mirror line or centre before you move. Reflecting (3, 4) in the y-axis gives (−3, 4), and a 90° turn clockwise about the origin takes (x, y) to (y, −x). To enlarge about a centre, multiply the step from the centre to the point, then add it back on: (3, 2) from centre (1, 1) by scale factor 3 is (7, 4).

List every outcome so each one is equally likely. A coin and a spinner numbered 1 to 3 give H1, H2, H3, T1, T2 and T3, six outcomes. When order does not matter, a pair like AB is the same as BA, so count it once.

The total is the group you are picking from at that moment. If 1 of 10 sweets is eaten, the next pick is out of 9. If you are told the person wears glasses, the total is only the people who wear glasses.

Class width is the upper boundary take away the lower one, and frequency density is frequency ÷ class width: 10 ≤ x < 40 has width 30, so frequency 60 gives density 2. The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, not the largest value minus the smallest.
Add or subtract the top numbers, then the bottom numbers: (2, 5) − (3, 1) = (−1, 4). To go from P to Q, go back to O and then out again, so PQ = −p + q.
Sequences start at n = 1, so test a rule by putting n = 1 and n = 2 back in: for 2, 7, 12, … the rule 5n − 3 gives 2, then 7. Counting from 3 to 6 including both ends gives 4 numbers, not 3.
Before you write the answer, reread the last line of the question. If a = 5 and it asks for 3a − 2, then 5 is only a step and 13 is the answer.
